The Chen-Rubin conjecture in a continuous setting

Christian Berg    Henrik L. Pedersen Note: Research supported by the Carlsberg Foundation
August 24, 2026
Abstract

We study the median m⁡(x)m(x) in the gamma distribution with parameter xx and show that 0<m′​(x)<10<m^{\prime}(x)<1 for all x>0x>0. This proves a generalization of a conjecture of Chen and Rubin from 1986: The sequence m⁡(n)−nm(n)-n decreases for n≥1n\geq 1. We also describe the asymptotic behaviour of mm and m′m^{\prime} at zero and at infinity.

2000 Mathematics Subject Classification:
primary 60E05; secondary 41A60, 33B15.

Keywords: median, gamma function, gamma distribution.

1 Introduction

The gamma distribution with parameter xx has density with respect to Lebesgue measure on (0,∞)(0,\infty) given by e−t​tx−1/Γ⁡(x)e^{-t}t^{x-1}/\Gamma(x). We consider the median m⁡(x)m(x) of this distribution which is defined implicitly as

∫0m⁡(x)e−t​tx−1Γ⁡(x)​𝑑t=12,\int_{0}^{m(x)}\frac{e^{-t}t^{x-1}}{\Gamma(x)}\,dt=\frac{1}{2},

or

∫0m⁡(x)e−t​tx−1​𝑑t=12​∫0∞e−t​tx−1​𝑑t.\int_{0}^{m(x)}e^{-t}t^{x-1}\,dt=\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-t}t^{x-1}\,dt. (1)

We of course also have

∫m⁡(x)∞e−t​tx−1​𝑑t=12​∫0∞e−t​tx−1​𝑑t.\int_{m(x)}^{\infty}e^{-t}t^{x-1}\,dt=\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-t}t^{x-1}\,dt. (2)

We show that mm is continuous and increasing. This is a consequence of a result about general convolution semigroups of probabilities on the positive half-line, that we give in Section 2. There we also show that mm is real analytic and that mm satisfies a certain differential equation.

We shall mainly study mm through the function

φ⁡(x)≡log⁡xm⁡(x),x>0.\varphi(x)\equiv\log\frac{x}{m(x)},\quad{x>0}. (3)

This function appears if we make the substitution u=log⁡(x/t)u=\log(x/t) in the relation (2). We get:

∫−∞φ⁡(x)e−x⁡(e−u+u)​𝑑u=12​∫−∞∞e−x⁡(e−u+u)​𝑑u.\int_{-\infty}^{\varphi(x)}e^{-x(e^{-u}+u)}\,du=\frac{1}{2}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{-x(e^{-u}+u)}\,du. (4)

Chen and Rubin (see [5]) studied the median of the gamma distribution and proved that x−1/3<m⁡(x)<xx-1/3<m(x)<x for x>0x>0. The relation (4) was also used in [5] to establish that φ⁡(x)>0\varphi(x)>0, or equivalently m⁡(x)<xm(x)<x. (It follows by observing that ∫−∞0e−x⁡(e−u+u)​𝑑u<∫0∞e−x⁡(e−u+u)​𝑑u\int_{-\infty}^{0}e^{-x(e^{-u}+u)}\,du<\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-x(e^{-u}+u)}\,du, which is true because sinh⁡u>u\sinh u>u for u>0u>0.)

Chen and Rubin furthermore conjectured that the sequence m⁡(n)−nm(n)-n decreases. This conjecture has recently been verified by Alzer (see [1]). He proved that m⁡(n+1)−α​nm(n+1)-\alpha n decreases for all n≥0n\geq 0 exactly when α≥1\alpha\geq 1 and increases exactly when α≤m⁡(2)−log⁡2\alpha\leq m(2)-\log 2. Note that m⁡(1)=log⁡2m(1)=\log 2.

In this paper we investigate the properties of mm as a function on (0,∞)(0,\infty). Chen and Rubin’s conjecture follows from the relation

m′​(x)​<1for allx>​0m^{\prime}(x)<1\quad\text{for all}\quad x>0

and it is our main goal to verify this relation. (See Theorem 3.3.)

We have drawn the graph of mm in Figure 1. (The dotted line is given by x−1/3x-1/3.)

In terms of φ\varphi Chen and Rubins conjecture takes the form 1−x​φ′​(x)<eφ⁡(x)1-x\varphi^{\prime}(x)<e^{\varphi(x)}. As a crucial step towards this result we show that x​φ​(x)x\varphi(x) decreases and that

13<x​φ​(x)<log⁡2\frac{1}{3}<x\varphi(x)<\log 2

for all x>0x>0 (see Proposition 3.5). In terms of mm this relation can be rewritten as

xe−log2/x<m(x)<xe−1/3x.xe^{-\log 2/x}<m(x)<xe^{-1/3x}.

If we use that e−a<1−a+a2/2e^{-a}<1-a+a^{2}/2 for a>0a>0 then we see that in fact

m⁡(x)<x⁡(1−13​x+118​x2)=x−13+118​xm(x)<x\left(1-\frac{1}{3x}+\frac{1}{18x^{2}}\right)=x-\frac{1}{3}+\frac{1}{18x}

for all x>0x>0. This result improves a result of Choi about m⁡(n+1)m(n+1), see [6, Theorem 1], even though it is there claimed to be best possible.

The asymptotic behaviour of m⁡(x)m(x) for x→0x\to 0 and for x→∞x\to\infty is given in Section 4. From this we can deduce that m(k)​(x)>0m^{(k)}(x)>0 for xx close to 0 for each kk while (−1)k​m(k)​(x)>0(-1)^{k}m^{(k)}(x)>0 for xx sufficiently large and k≥2k\geq 2. It is reasonable to believe that m′′​(x)>0m^{\prime\prime}(x)>0 for all x>0x>0, i.e. mm is convex, but the higher derivatives of odd order change sign.

We also relate our work to papers of Ramanujan, Watson and others on Ramanujan’s rational approximation to exe^{x}, see Section 6.

2 Medians of convolution semigroups on the half-line

A family {μx}x>0\{\mu_{x}\}_{x>0} of probabilities concentrated on [0,∞)[0,\infty) is called a convolution semigroup if it has the properties

  1. (i)

    μx​([0,∞))=1\mu_{x}([0,\infty))=1 for all x>0x>0;

  2. (ii)

    μx∗μy=μx+y\mu_{x}\ast\mu_{y}=\mu_{x+y} for all x,y>0x,y>0;

  3. (iii)

    μx→δ0\mu_{x}\to\delta_{0} for x→0x\to 0 in the vague topology (here δ0\delta_{0} denotes the Dirac mass at zero).

The gamma distributions {e−t​tx−1/Γ⁡(x)​d​t}x>0\{e^{-t}t^{x-1}/\Gamma(x)\,dt\}_{x>0} is an example of such a convolution semigroup.

A probability measure μ\mu on [0,∞)[0,\infty) has median mm if

μ⁡([0,m])=12.\mu([0,m])=\frac{1}{2}.

Of course a probability measure may not have a median and if it exists it may not be unique. However, if the measure has density w.r.t. Lebesgue measure on [0,∞)[0,\infty) then the median exists: this follows from the fact that M→μ⁡([0,M])M\to\mu([0,M]) is continuous and increases from 0 to 1. If the density is strictly positive almost everywhere on [0,∞)[0,\infty) then the median is unique.

Proposition 2.1

Let {μx}x>0\{\mu_{x}\}_{x>0} be a convolution semigroup of probabilities on [0,∞)[0,\infty) having a.e. strictly positive densities w.r.t. Lebesgue measure on [0,∞)[0,\infty). Then the median m⁡(x)m(x) of μx\mu_{x} is a continuous and strictly increasing function on (0,∞)(0,\infty).

Proof. We write d​μx​(t)=gx​(t)​d​td\mu_{x}(t)=g_{x}(t)\,dt. As we have seen above, mm exists as a function on the positive half-line. We now show that mm is increasing. Let x>0x>0 and h>0h>0. Then

∫0m⁡(x)gx+h​(t)​𝑑t\displaystyle\int_{0}^{m(x)}g_{x+h}(t)\,dt =\displaystyle= ∫0m⁡(x)gx∗gh​(t)​𝑑t\displaystyle\int_{0}^{m(x)}g_{x}\ast g_{h}(t)\,dt
=\displaystyle= ∫0m⁡(x)∫0tgh​(t−s)​gx​(s)​𝑑s​𝑑t\displaystyle\int_{0}^{m(x)}\int_{0}^{t}g_{h}(t-s)g_{x}(s)\,ds\,dt
=\displaystyle= ∫0m⁡(x)∫sm⁡(x)gh​(t−s)​𝑑t​gx​(s)​𝑑s\displaystyle\int_{0}^{m(x)}\int_{s}^{m(x)}g_{h}(t-s)\,dt\,g_{x}(s)\,ds
=\displaystyle= ∫0m⁡(x)∫0m⁡(x)−sgh​(t)​𝑑t​gx​(s)​𝑑s\displaystyle\int_{0}^{m(x)}\int_{0}^{m(x)-s}g_{h}(t)\,dt\,g_{x}(s)\,ds
<\displaystyle< ∫0m⁡(x)∫0∞gh​(t)​𝑑t​gx​(s)​𝑑s\displaystyle\int_{0}^{m(x)}\int_{0}^{\infty}g_{h}(t)\,dt\,g_{x}(s)\,ds
=\displaystyle= ∫0m⁡(x)gx​(s)​𝑑s=12.\displaystyle\int_{0}^{m(x)}g_{x}(s)\,ds\quad=\quad\frac{1}{2}.

Since m⁡(x+h)m(x+h) by definition satisfies

∫0m⁡(x+h)gx+h​(t)​𝑑t=12,\int_{0}^{m(x+h)}g_{x+h}(t)\,dt=\frac{1}{2},

we must therefore have m⁡(x)<m⁡(x+h)m(x)<m(x+h). This shows that mm is strictly increasing.

Concerning the continuity we first notice that for any A>0A>0,

∫0Agx0+h​(t)​𝑑t→∫0Agx0​(t)​𝑑t\int_{0}^{A}g_{x_{0}+h}(t)\,dt\to\int_{0}^{A}g_{x_{0}}(t)\,dt

as h→0h\to 0. In fact, using the same computation as above we get

∫0Agx0+h​(t)​𝑑t\displaystyle\int_{0}^{A}g_{x_{0}+h}(t)\,dt =\displaystyle= ∫0Agx0∗gh​(t)​𝑑t\displaystyle\int_{0}^{A}g_{x_{0}}\ast g_{h}(t)\,dt
=\displaystyle= ∫0A∫0A−sgh​(t)​𝑑t​gx0​(s)​𝑑s\displaystyle\int_{0}^{A}\int_{0}^{A-s}g_{h}(t)\,dt\,g_{x_{0}}(s)\,ds
→\displaystyle\to ∫0A∫0A−sd​δ0​(t)​gx0​(s)​𝑑s\displaystyle\int_{0}^{A}\int_{0}^{A-s}\,d\delta_{0}(t)\,g_{x_{0}}(s)\,ds
=\displaystyle= ∫0Agx0​(s)​𝑑s,\displaystyle\int_{0}^{A}g_{x_{0}}(s)\,ds,

as h→0h\to 0, because of the vague convergence. (All measures have the same total mass, so vague convergence implies weak convergence.) Now let x0>0x_{0}>0 and let ϵ>0\epsilon>0 be given. For A=m⁡(x0)+ϵA=m(x_{0})+\epsilon we have, as h→0+h\to 0_{+},

∫0m⁡(x0)+ϵgx0+h​(t)​𝑑t→∫0m⁡(x0)+ϵgx0​(t)​𝑑t>12,\int_{0}^{m(x_{0})+\epsilon}g_{x_{0}+h}(t)\,dt\to\int_{0}^{m(x_{0})+\epsilon}g_{x_{0}}(t)\,dt>\frac{1}{2},

so that m⁡(x0+h)≤m⁡(x0)+ϵm(x_{0}+h)\leq m(x_{0})+\epsilon for all sufficiently small and positive hh. Similarly we find m⁡(x0−h)≥m⁡(x0)−ϵm(x_{0}-h)\geq m(x_{0})-\epsilon, and this shows that mm is continuous. □\square

We now specialize to consider the medians m⁡(x)m(x) of the gamma distributions. We notice

Proposition 2.2

The median m⁡(x)m(x) of the gamma distributions is real analytic.

Proof. We consider the C1C^{1}-function

F⁡(x,y)=∫0ye−t​tx−1​1Γ⁡(x)​𝑑t,x,y>0.F(x,y)=\int_{0}^{y}e^{-t}t^{x-1}\frac{1}{\Gamma(x)}\,dt,\quad x,y>0.

The median is implicitly defined as F⁡(x,m⁡(x))=1/2F(x,m(x))=1/2. The fact that the continuous function mm is C1C^{1} follows from the implicit function theorem, which yields the following differential equation for mm:

e−m⁡(x)​m​(x)x−1​m′​(x)=12​Γ′​(x)−∫0m⁡(x)(log⁡t)​e−t​tx−1​𝑑t,e^{-m(x)}m(x)^{x-1}m^{\prime}(x)=\frac{1}{2}\Gamma^{\prime}(x)-\int_{0}^{m(x)}(\log t)\,e^{-t}t^{x-1}\,dt, (5)

which shows that mm satisfies a differential equation of the form

m′​(x)=G⁡(x,m⁡(x)),m^{\prime}(x)=G(x,m(x)),

with G⁡(x,y)G(x,y) being real analytic for x,y>0x,y>0. Therefore mm is real analytic. □\square

Remark 2.3

From (5) it seems difficult to deduce monotonicity properties of mm; e.g. it is not at all clear that m′​(x)>0m^{\prime}(x)>0, which we know from Proposition 2.1. For another derivation of m′​(x)>0m^{\prime}(x)>0 see Proposition 3.5.

3 Uniform results

In this section we prove the generalized version of Chen and Rubin’s conjecture (Theorem 3.3).

Proposition 3.2 below is the key to our results. Before stating it we need some notation.

We consider the function f⁡(x)=e−x+xf(x)=e^{-x}+x. It is easily seen that f⁡(x)f(x) decreases for x<0x<0 and then increases for x>0x>0. Hence ff has an inverse on (−∞,0](-\infty,0], which we call uu, and an inverse on [0,∞)[0,\infty), which we call vv. The function uu is defined for t≥1t\geq 1 as u⁡(t)≤0u(t)\leq 0 and

e−u⁡(t)+u⁡(t)=t,t≥1;e^{-u(t)}+u(t)=t,\quad t\geq 1;

the function vv as v⁡(t)≥0v(t)\geq 0 and

e−v⁡(t)+v⁡(t)=t,t≥1.e^{-v(t)}+v(t)=t,\quad t\geq 1.

The following function ξ\xi plays an important role:

ξ⁡(t)=11−e−v⁡(t)+11−e−u⁡(t)=u′​(t)+v′​(t).\xi(t)=\frac{1}{1-e^{-v(t)}}+\frac{1}{1-e^{-u(t)}}=u^{\prime}(t)+v^{\prime}(t). (6)

The function ξ⁡(t)\xi(t) is defined for t>1t>1 by (6), but for t=1t=1 this expression yields ∞−∞\infty-\infty and a closer study is necessary. The following result holds and will be proved in Section 5.

Proposition 3.1

The function ξ⁡(t)\xi(t) defined for t>1t>1 by (6) has a holomorphic extension to the cut plane ℂ∖{x±2​π​i|x≥1}\mathbb{C}\setminus\{x\pm 2\pi i\,|\,x\geq 1\}. The following holds:

  1. (i)

    limt→−∞ξ⁡(t)=0\lim_{t\to-\infty}\xi(t)=0, limt→∞ξ⁡(t)=1\lim_{t\to\infty}\xi(t)=1, ξ⁡(t)\xi(t) is increasing;

  2. (ii)

    limt→∞ξ(n)​(t)=0\lim_{t\to\infty}\xi^{(n)}(t)=0 for n≥1n\geq 1;

  3. (iii)

    ξ⁡(t)\xi(t) is concave for t∈[1,∞)t\in[1,\infty);

  4. (iv)

    ξ⁡(1)=2/3\xi(1)=2/3, ξ′​(1)=8/135\xi^{\prime}(1)=8/135 and ξ′′(1)=−16/2835\xi^{\prime\prime}(1)=-16/2835.

  5. (v)

    All points on {x±2​π​i|x≥1}\{x\pm 2\pi i\,|\,x\geq 1\} are singular points for ξ\xi and the series

    ∑k=0∞ξ(k)​(1)xk+1\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{\xi^{(k)}(1)}{x^{k+1}}

    diverges for all xx.

In Figure 2 we have shown the graph of ξ⁡(t)\xi(t) for t≥1t\geq 1.

We have

The difference between eφ⁡(x)e^{\varphi(x)} and 1+φ⁡(x)+12​φ​(x)21+\varphi(x)+\frac{1}{2}\varphi(x)^{2} is O⁡(φ​(x)3)O(\varphi(x)^{3}), that is (by Proposition 3.5) the difference is O⁡(x−3)O(x^{-3}). 5 Properties of the auxiliary function ξ\xi

In this section we derive the properties of the function ξ\xi, stated in Proposition 3.1. Most of these properties we found surprisingly difficult to establish. Much of the difficulty lies in the fact that ξ\xi in given as a sum of two terms, where it is necessary to control the cancellation between these two terms.

Throughout this section uu and vv denote the functions defined in (6). We begin by considering them separately. The investigation is based on a simple lemma of independent interest. We recall that a C∞C^{\infty}-function ν⁡(t)\nu(t) defined on the positive half-line is called completely monotonic if

(−1)p​ν(p)​(t)≥0,for all integersp≥0.(-1)^{p}\nu^{(p)}(t)\geq 0,\quad\text{for all integers}\quad p\geq 0.

It is called a Bernstein function if

ν⁡(t)≥0and(−1)p​ν(p)​(t)≤0,for all integersp≥1.\nu(t)\geq 0\quad\text{and}\quad(-1)^{p}\nu^{(p)}(t)\leq 0,\quad\text{for all integers}\quad p\geq 1.

The last conditions can also be expressed that ν′​(t)\nu^{\prime}(t) is completely monotonic. For details about these classes of functions see e.g. [3].

Lemma 5.1

Let FF be completely monotonic, let ς⁡(t)\varsigma(t) be a positive C∞C^{\infty}-function for t>0t>0 and assume that ς′​(t)=F⁡(ς⁡(t))\varsigma^{\prime}(t)=F(\varsigma(t)). Then we have:

For each n≥1n\geq 1 there exists a completely monotonic function FnF_{n} such that

(−1)n−1​ς(n)​(t)=Fn​(ς⁡(t)).(-1)^{n-1}\varsigma^{(n)}(t)=F_{n}(\varsigma(t)).

In particular ς\varsigma is a Bernstein function.

Proof. For n=1n=1 we can use F1=FF_{1}=F. If (−1)n−1​ς(n)​(t)=Fn​(ς⁡(t))(-1)^{n-1}\varsigma^{(n)}(t)=F_{n}(\varsigma(t)) for some completely monotonic function FnF_{n} then

(−1)n​ς(n+1)​(t)=−Fn′​(ς⁡(t))​ς′​(t)=−Fn′​(ς⁡(t))​F​(ς⁡(t)).(-1)^{n}\varsigma^{(n+1)}(t)=-F_{n}^{\prime}(\varsigma(t))\varsigma^{\prime}(t)=-F_{n}^{\prime}(\varsigma(t))F(\varsigma(t)).

Here Fn+1≡−Fn′​FF_{n+1}\equiv-F_{n}^{\prime}F is completely monotonic as a product of two completely monotonic fuctions.

Furthermore we have

(−1)n​ς(n)​(t)=−Fn​(ς⁡(t))≤0,(-1)^{n}\varsigma^{(n)}(t)=-F_{n}(\varsigma(t))\leq 0,

so ς\varsigma is a Bernstein function. □\square

Proposition 5.2

The functions −u⁡(t+1)-u(t+1) and v⁡(t+1)v(t+1) are Bernstein functions and

limt→∞v⁡(t)/t=1,limt→∞u⁡(t)/t=0.\lim_{t\to\infty}v(t)/t=1,\quad\lim_{t\to\infty}u(t)/t=0.

Proof. We have v′​(t)=F⁡(v⁡(t))v^{\prime}(t)=F(v(t)) where

F⁡(x)=11−e−x=∑k=0∞e−k​xF(x)=\frac{1}{1-e^{-x}}=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}e^{-kx}

is completely monotonic. Since v⁡(t)→∞v(t)\to\infty as t→∞t\to\infty we have e−v⁡(t)→0e^{-v(t)}\to 0 and hence v⁡(t)/t=1−e−v⁡(t)/t→1v(t)/t=1-e^{-v(t)}/t\to 1 as t→∞t\to\infty.

For the function w≡−uw\equiv-u we have w′​(t)=G⁡(w⁡(t))w^{\prime}(t)=G(w(t)) where

G⁡(x)=1ex−1=∑k=1∞e−k​xG(x)=\frac{1}{e^{x}-1}=\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}e^{-kx}

is completely monotonic. We have t=e−u⁡(t)+u⁡(t)>1+u​(t)2/2t=e^{-u(t)}+u(t)>1+u(t)^{2}/2 (since u⁡(t)<0u(t)<0) so that −u⁡(t)<2​(t−1)-u(t)<\sqrt{2(t-1)} and thus u⁡(t)/t→0u(t)/t\to 0 as t→∞t\to\infty. □\square

Bernstein functions admit integral representations (see e.g. [3, p. 64]) and thus we have

v⁡(t+1)=t+∫0∞(1−e−x​t)​𝑑λ​(x)v(t+1)=t+\int_{0}^{\infty}(1-e^{-xt})\,d\lambda(x)

and

−u⁡(t+1)=∫0∞(1−e−x​t)​𝑑σ​(x),-u(t+1)=\int_{0}^{\infty}(1-e^{-xt})\,d\sigma(x),

for some positive measures λ\lambda and σ\sigma on (0,∞)(0,\infty). Since t+1−v⁡(t+1)=e−v⁡(t+1)→0t+1-v(t+1)=e^{-v(t+1)}\to 0 for t→∞t\to\infty we conclude that λ⁡((,,,))=1\lambda((0,\infty))=1, hence

v⁡(t+1)=t+1−∫0∞e−x​t​𝑑λ​(x).v(t+1)=t+1-\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-xt}\,d\lambda(x).

The measure σ\sigma has infinite total mass because u⁡(t)→−∞u(t)\to-\infty for t→∞t\to\infty.

From these representations we see that ξ⁡(t)=u′​(t)+v′​(t)→1\xi(t)=u^{\prime}(t)+v^{\prime}(t)\to 1 as t→∞t\to\infty and also that u(n+1)​(t)u^{(n+1)}(t) and v(n+1)​(t)v^{(n+1)}(t) both tend to zero as tt tends to infinity for any n≥1n\geq 1. This shows that ξ(n)​(t)=u(n+1)​(t)+v(n+1)​(t)→0\xi^{(n)}(t)=u^{(n+1)}(t)+v^{(n+1)}(t)\to 0 as t→∞t\to\infty for any n≥1n\geq 1.

One could hope to deduce further properties of ξ\xi by using these integral representations. We have not succeeded in doing this, since much cancellation between uu and vv takes place and we do not know λ\lambda and σ\sigma explicitly. Furthermore, it it not even true that ξ⁡(t+1)\xi(t+1) is a Bernstein function even though it is increasing and concave.

We have found an approach using complex analysis and we shall make extensive use of the theory of the so-called Pick functions, see [7]. A holomorphic function pp defined in the upper half plane is a Pick function if it maps the upper half plane into the closed upper half plane, or put in another way, if ℑ⁡p\Im p is a non-negative harmonic function. A Pick function has an integral representation,

p⁡(z)=a​z+b+∫−∞∞(1t−z−tt2+1)​𝑑μ​(t),p(z)=az+b+\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\left(\frac{1}{t-z}-\frac{t}{t^{2}+1}\right)\,d\mu(t), (13)

where a≥0a\geq 0, bb is real and μ\mu is a positive measure on the real line. Furthermore,

a=limy→∞ℑ⁡p⁡(i​y)y,b=ℜ⁡p⁡(i)a=\lim_{y\to\infty}\frac{\Im p(iy)}{y},\quad b=\Re p(i)

and

μ=limy→0+ℑ⁡p⁡(x+i​y)π​d​x\mu=\lim_{y\to 0_{+}}\frac{\Im p(x+iy)}{\pi}dx

in the vague topology. Note that a Pick function can be extended to a holomorphic function in ℂ∖ℝ\mathbb{C}\setminus\mathbb{R} by (13). If A⊆ℝA\subseteq\mathbb{R} is closed we recall that pp has a holomorphic extension to ℂ∖A\mathbb{C}\setminus A if and only if the support of μ\mu is contained in AA.

The proofs of the results to follow are based on an investigation of the holomorphic function

f⁡(z)=e−z+z.f(z)=e^{-z}+z. (14)

Concerning the values of the function ξ\xi and its derivatives at z=1z=1 we have the following proposition.

Proposition 5.3

The function ξ⁡(z)\xi(z) is holomorphic in a neighbourhood of z=1z=1 and we have ξ⁡(1)=2/3\xi(1)=2/3 and ξ′​(1)=8/135\xi^{\prime}(1)=8/135.

Remark 5.4

One can in principle find any derivative of ξ\xi at 1 in this way. Computations show that ξ′′(1)=−16/2835\xi^{\prime\prime}(1)=-16/2835. The higher order derivatives of ξ\xi at 1 can be found in the appendix.

The monotonicity properties of ξ\xi follows from the next proposition.

Proposition 5.5

The function ξ\xi increases on the real line and it is concave on [1,∞)[1,\infty).

The key to the proof of this proposition is an integral representation of ξ\xi that we give in Proposition 5.12.

The function f⁡(z)=e−z+zf(z)=e^{-z}+z is a conformal mapping of the strip

e−x​cos⁡y+x\displaystyle e^{-x}\cos y+x =\displaystyle= σ\displaystyle\sigma

Lemma 5.8

The function

has a holomorphic extension to ℂ∖{ℑ⁡w=±2​π​i,ℜ⁡w≥1}\mathbb{C}\setminus\{\Im w=\pm 2\pi i,\Re w\geq 1\}.

For t>1t>1 we have g⁡(t)=u⁡(t)+v⁡(t)g(t)=u(t)+v(t) and g′​(t)=ξ​(t)g^{\prime}(t)=\xi(t). The function g′g^{\prime} is thus a holomorphic extension of ξ\xi.

All points on the lines {ℑ⁡w=±2​π​i,ℜ⁡w≥1}\{\Im w=\pm 2\pi i,\Re w\geq 1\} are singular points for gg.

Proof. Since f−1f^{-1} is a conformal mapping of the region

Concerning the boundary values on the half-lines {ℑ⁡w=±2​π​i,ℜ⁡w≥1}\{\Im w=\pm 2\pi i,\Re w\geq 1\} we have (σ≥1\sigma\geq 1)

=\displaystyle= v⁡(σ)+2​π​i+f−1​(σ−2​π​i)¯\displaystyle v(\sigma)+2\pi i+\overline{f^{-1}(\sigma-2\pi i)}

{ℑ⁡w=2​π​i,ℜ⁡w≥1}\{\Im w=2\pi i,\Re w\geq 1\}

and so all these points are singular points. Since g⁡(w)=g⁡(w¯)¯g(w)=\overline{g(\overline{w})} the same conclusion holds for the points on the other half-line. □\square

Proposition 5.9

The Taylor series for ξ⁡(z)\xi(z) centered at 1 has radius of convergence equal to 2​π2\pi and the asymptotic series

∑k=0∞ξ(k)​(1)zk\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{\xi^{(k)}(1)}{z^{k}}

diverges for any zz in ℂ\mathbb{C}.

Proof. We have ξ=g′\xi=g^{\prime}, where gg is the function in Lemma 5.8. If the radius of convergence of ξ\xi at 1 were larger than 2​π2\pi then the primitive gg would also have a holomorhic extension to this larger disk, and this contradicts the fact that gg has singular points in that disk.

Concerning the divergence of the asymptotic series we use that the radius of convergence of the Taylor series is finite. It means that

lim supk→∞(|ξ(k)​(1)|k!)1/k>0,\limsup_{k\to\infty}\left(\frac{|\xi^{(k)}(1)|}{k!}\right)^{1/k}>0,

and hence that for some ϵ>0\epsilon>0, |ξ(k)​(1)|1/k/(k!)1/k>ϵ|\xi^{(k)}(1)|^{1/k}/(k!)^{1/k}>\epsilon for infinitely many kk. From Stirlings formula we have (k!)1/k∼k/e(k!)^{1/k}\sim k/e and therefore

lim supk→∞|ξ(k)​(1)|1/k=∞.\limsup_{k\to\infty}|\xi^{(k)}(1)|^{1/k}=\infty.

This shows on the other hand that the asymptotic series diverges for any complex number zz. □\square

In the following log\log denotes the principal logarithm defined in the cut plane ℂ∖(−∞,0]\mathbb{C}\setminus(-\infty,0].

Lemma 5.10

The function

Ψ⁡(w)=g⁡(log⁡w)=f−1​(log⁡w)+f−1​(log⁡w¯)¯\Psi(w)=g(\log w)=f^{-1}(\log w)+\overline{f^{-1}(\log\overline{w})}

is a Pick function. It has the representation

Ψ⁡(w)=ℜ⁡Ψ⁡(i)−∫0∞(1t+w−tt2+1)​h​(t)​𝑑t,\Psi(w)=\Re\Psi(i)-\int_{0}^{\infty}\left(\frac{1}{t+w}-\frac{t}{t^{2}+1}\right)\,h(t)dt,

h⁡(t)=1−ℑ⁡f−1​(log⁡t−i​π)π.h(t)=1-\frac{\Im\,f^{-1}(\log t-i\pi)}{\pi}.

Furthermore, hh increases on (0,∞)(0,\infty) from 0 to 1.

For τ∈[e,∞)\tau\in[e,\infty) we have

Ψ⁡(τ)=u⁡(log⁡τ)+v⁡(log⁡τ).\Psi(\tau)=u(\log\tau)+v(\log\tau).

Proof. We consider the holomorphic function gg from Lemma 5.8 in the strip 𝒮={0<ℑw<π}\mathcal{S}=\{0<\Im w<\pi\}. Hence the function V⁡(w)=ℑ⁡g⁡(w)V(w)=\Im g(w) is a harmonic function in 𝒮\mathcal{S}. Furthermore, since f−1f^{-1} maps all of {ℑw<π}∖{x|x≥1}\{\Im w<\pi\}\setminus\{x\,|\,x\geq 1\} into 𝒮\mathcal{S}, VV is also bounded there, with the apriori bound −π<V⁡(w)<π-\pi<V(w)<\pi. We claim that indeed 0<V⁡(w)<π0<V(w)<\pi for all w∈𝒮w\in\mathcal{S}.

We consider the boundary values of VV. The horizontal line {t+iπ,|t∈ℝ}\{t+i\pi,\,|\,t\in\mathbb{R}\} is mapped by f−1f^{-1} to itself, whereas {t−iπ,|t∈ℝ}\{t-i\pi,\,|\,t\in\mathbb{R}\} is mapped by f−1f^{-1} to some curve inside the strip 𝒮\mathcal{S}. Ψ⁡(w)=ℜ⁡Ψ⁡(i)+∫−∞∞(1t−w−tt2+1)​𝑑μ​(t),\Psi(w)=\Re\Psi(i)+\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\left(\frac{1}{t-w}-\frac{t}{t^{2}+1}\right)\,d\mu(t),

for some positive measure μ\mu. Here ℑ⁡Ψ⁡(t)=0\Im\Psi(t)=0 for t>0t>0 since VV is zero on the real line. We thus find the measure μ\mu to be supported on the negative half-line with density

1−ℑ⁡f−1​(log⁡(−t)−i​π)π,t<0.1-\frac{\Im\,f^{-1}(\log(-t)-i\pi)}{\pi},\quad t<0.

After making a change of variable (t↦−tt\mapsto-t) in the integral we conclude that

where hh is the function in the statement of the lemma.

By definition of hh, π⁡(1−h⁡(t))=ℑ⁡f−1​(log⁡t−i​π)\pi(1-h(t))=\Im f^{-1}(\log t-i\pi), so hh is increasing if the solution Y⁡(t)Y(t) to the equation F−π​(Y⁡(t))=log⁡tF_{-\pi}(Y(t))=\log t is decreasing. This is indeed the case, since

F−π′​(Y⁡(t))​Y′​(t)=1t>0,F_{-\pi}^{\prime}(Y(t))Y^{\prime}(t)=\frac{1}{t}>0,

ξ⁡(log⁡w)=∫0∞wt+w​h′​(t)​𝑑t,\xi(\log w)=\int_{0}^{\infty}\frac{w}{t+w}\,h^{\prime}(t)\,dt,

ξ⁡(log⁡w)=1−∫0∞tt+w​h′​(t)​𝑑t.\xi(\log w)=1-\int_{0}^{\infty}\frac{t}{t+w}\,h^{\prime}(t)\,dt.

□\square

Proof of Proposition 5.5. We get by differentiation of the formula in Proposition 5.12 that

ξ′​(log⁡w)w=∫0∞t(t+w)2​h′​(t)​𝑑t,\frac{\xi^{\prime}(\log w)}{w}=\int_{0}^{\infty}\frac{t}{(t+w)^{2}}\,h^{\prime}(t)\,dt,

and since we know that h′​(t)>0h^{\prime}(t)>0 for all t∈ℝt\in\mathbb{R}, we see that ξ′​(t)>0\xi^{\prime}(t)>0 for all t∈ℝt\in\mathbb{R}.

It is more technical to establish that ξ⁡(t)\xi(t) is concave for t≥1t\geq 1. We differentiate both sides of the relation above once more and we get in this way

ξ′′(logw)−ξ′(logw)=−2w2∫0∞t(t+w)3h′(t)dt,\xi^{\prime\prime}(\log w)-\xi^{\prime}(\log w)=-2w^{2}\int_{0}^{\infty}\frac{t}{(t+w)^{3}}\,h^{\prime}(t)\,dt,

=\displaystyle= ∫0∞t−w(t+w)3​w​t​h′​(t)​𝑑t\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\infty}\frac{t-w}{(t+w)^{3}}\,wth^{\prime}(t)\,dt
=\displaystyle= w​∫0∞s−1(s+1)3​s​h′​(s​w)​𝑑s.\displaystyle w\int_{0}^{\infty}\frac{s-1}{(s+1)^{3}}\,sh^{\prime}(sw)\,ds.

This last integral we split into two, one for s<1s<1 and another for s>1s>1. We thus get, after making the substitution s→1/ss\to 1/s in the latter one,

ξ′′​(log⁡w)w\displaystyle\frac{\xi^{\prime\prime}(\log w)}{w} =\displaystyle= ∫01s−1(s+1)3​s​h′​(s​w)​𝑑s+∫011/s−1(1/s+1)3​1s​h′​(ws)​d​ss2\displaystyle\int_{0}^{1}\frac{s-1}{(s+1)^{3}}\,sh^{\prime}(sw)\,ds+\int_{0}^{1}\frac{1/s-1}{(1/s+1)^{3}}\,\frac{1}{s}h^{\prime}\left(\frac{w}{s}\right)\,\frac{ds}{s^{2}}
=\displaystyle= ∫011−s(1+s)3​(1s​h′​(ws)−s​h′​(s​w))​𝑑s.\displaystyle\int_{0}^{1}\frac{1-s}{(1+s)^{3}}\,\left(\frac{1}{s}h^{\prime}\left(\frac{w}{s}\right)-sh^{\prime}(sw)\right)\,ds.

From this relation we see that ξ\xi is concave on [log⁡w0,∞)[\log w_{0},\infty) if

1s​h′​(ws)−s​h′​(s​w)≤0fors∈(0,1)andw≥w0.\frac{1}{s}h^{\prime}\left(\frac{w}{s}\right)-sh^{\prime}(sw)\leq 0\quad\text{for}\quad s\in(0,1)\quad\text{and}\quad w\geq w_{0}. (17)

Now, as noted in the proof of Lemma 5.10, h⁡(s)=1−Y−π​(log⁡s)/πh(s)=1-Y_{-\pi}(\log s)/\pi, where Y−π​(t)∈(0,π)Y_{-\pi}(t)\in(0,\pi) is the solution to the equation F−π​(Y−π​(t))=tF_{-\pi}(Y_{-\pi}(t))=t, see (15). and

s​h′​(s​w)=−Y−π′​(log⁡w+log⁡s)π​w.sh^{\prime}(sw)=-\frac{Y_{-\pi}^{\prime}(\log w+\log s)}{\pi w}.

We see that (17) holds provided

Y−π′​(log⁡w−log⁡s)≥Y−π′​(log⁡w+log⁡s).Y_{-\pi}^{\prime}(\log w-\log s)\geq Y_{-\pi}^{\prime}(\log w+\log s).

Y−π′​(log⁡w+t)≥Y−π′​(log⁡w−t)Y_{-\pi}^{\prime}(\log w+t)\geq Y_{-\pi}^{\prime}(\log w-t)

for all t≥0t\geq 0 and all w≥w0w\geq w_{0}. We aim at proving this for w0=ew_{0}=e, so what we really should prove is the following:

Y−π′​(α+t)≥Y−π′​(α−t)Y_{-\pi}^{\prime}(\alpha+t)\geq Y_{-\pi}^{\prime}(\alpha-t) (18)

for all t≥0t\geq 0 and all α≥1\alpha\geq 1. We verify this inequality by using Lemma 5.7. According to that lemma, with w=1−α−t+i​πw=1-\alpha-t+i\pi, we have

6 Relation to work of Ramanujan

Defining θ⁡(n)\theta(n) for natural numbers nn by

en2=∑k=0n−1nkk!+θ⁡(n)​nnn!,\frac{e^{n}}{2}=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\frac{n^{k}}{k!}+\theta(n)\frac{n^{n}}{n!}, (19)

Ramanujan [11] claimed that 13<θ⁡(n)<12\frac{1}{3}<\theta(n)<\frac{1}{2}. This was later proved independently by Szegő [12] and Watson [13]. Further details about Ramanujan’s problem can be found in [4]. See also [8]. Choi noticed the relation between this problem and the median in the gamma distribution, see [6]. By nn partial integrations we get the formula

1n!​∫0ntn​e−t​𝑑t=1−e−n​∑k=0nnkk!,\frac{1}{n!}\int_{0}^{n}t^{n}e^{-t}\,dt=1-e^{-n}\sum_{k=0}^{n}\frac{n^{k}}{k!},

hence by (19)

1n!​∫0ntn​e−t​𝑑t=12−nnn!​(1−θ⁡(n))​e−n,\frac{1}{n!}\int_{0}^{n}t^{n}e^{-t}\,dt=\frac{1}{2}-\frac{n^{n}}{n!}(1-\theta(n))e^{-n},

and finally

1−θ⁡(n)=(en)n​∫nm⁡(n+1)tn​e−t​𝑑t.1-\theta(n)=\left(\frac{e}{n}\right)^{n}\int_{n}^{m(n+1)}t^{n}e^{-t}\,dt. (20)

Following Watson [13] we can write

θ⁡(n)\displaystyle\theta(n) =\displaystyle= 1+en2​nn​n!−n!nn​∑k=0nnkk!\displaystyle 1+\frac{e^{n}}{2n^{n}}n!-\frac{n!}{n^{n}}\sum_{k=0}^{n}\frac{n^{k}}{k!}
=\displaystyle= 1+en2​nn​∫0∞tn​e−t​𝑑t−1nn​∫0∞(n+t)n​e−t​𝑑t\displaystyle 1+\frac{e^{n}}{2n^{n}}\int_{0}^{\infty}t^{n}e^{-t}\,dt-\frac{1}{n^{n}}\int_{0}^{\infty}(n+t)^{n}e^{-t}\,dt
=\displaystyle= 1+n2​∫0∞tn​en⁡(1−t)​𝑑t−∫0∞(1+t/n)n​e−t​𝑑t.\displaystyle 1+\frac{n}{2}\int_{0}^{\infty}t^{n}e^{n(1-t)}\,dt-\int_{0}^{\infty}(1+t/n)^{n}e^{-t}\,dt.

We now make the substitution s=1+t/ns=1+t/n in the last integral and split the first integral in two by integrating over (0,1)(0,1) and (1,∞)(1,\infty). This gives

θ⁡(n)=1+n2​(∫01(t​e1−t)n​𝑑t−∫1∞(t​e1−t)n​𝑑t).\theta(n)=1+\frac{n}{2}\left(\int_{0}^{1}(te^{1-t})^{n}\,dt-\int_{1}^{\infty}(te^{1-t})^{n}\,dt\right). (21)

Watson notices that the right-hand side of this equation makes perfect sence when nn is replaced by a positive real variable xx and the corresponding function he denotes y⁡(x)y(x). We keep the notation θ⁡(x)\theta(x) and make the substitution t=e−ut=e^{-u} in the integrals to get

θ⁡(x)=1+x2​ex​(∫0∞e−x⁡(u+e−u)−u​𝑑u−∫−∞0e−x⁡(u+e−u)−u​𝑑u).\theta(x)=1+\frac{x}{2}e^{x}\left(\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-x(u+e^{-u})-u}\,du-\int_{-\infty}^{0}e^{-x(u+e^{-u})-u}\,du\right).

Introducing the functions u,vu,v from Section 3 we get

θ⁡(x)=1+x2​ex​∫1∞e−x​t​(e−v⁡(t)​v′​(t)+e−u⁡(t)​u′​(t))​𝑑t\theta(x)=1+\frac{x}{2}e^{x}\int_{1}^{\infty}e^{-xt}\left(e^{-v(t)}v^{\prime}(t)+e^{-u(t)}u^{\prime}(t)\right)\,dt

and using

e−v⁡(t)​v′​(t)+e−u⁡(t)​u′​(t)=ξ⁡(t)−2,e^{-v(t)}v^{\prime}(t)+e^{-u(t)}u^{\prime}(t)=\xi(t)-2,

we get after some calculation

θ⁡(x)=x2​∫0∞e−x​t​ξ​(t+1)​𝑑t=13+12​∫0∞e−x​t​ξ′​(t+1)​𝑑t.\theta(x)=\frac{x}{2}\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-xt}\xi(t+1)\,dt=\frac{1}{3}+\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-xt}\xi^{\prime}(t+1)\,dt. (22)

From (10) we get

θ⁡(x)=∑k=0nξ(k)​(1)2​xk+o⁡(x−n).\theta(x)=\sum_{k=0}^{n}\frac{\xi^{(k)}(1)}{2x^{k}}+o(x^{-n}).

We further see that the function ϕ⁡(t)\phi(t) from [13, p.300] is given as

ϕ⁡(t)=1358​ξ′​(t+1).\phi(t)=\frac{135}{8}\xi^{\prime}(t+1).

In [13] Watson discusses the behaviour of −t−1​log⁡ϕ​(t)-t^{-1}\log\phi(t) for t>0t>0. He reaches a conclusion using a combination of rigorous analysis and numerical tabulation. The present analysis does not contribute in making his conclusion rigorous.

7 Appendix: Higher order expansions and Maple code

In this section we give the derivatives of ξ\xi at 1 of order up to 10 and higher order asymptotic expansions of φ⁡(x)\varphi(x) and m⁡(x)m(x). These results we have found using the “Maple 9” system. We have also included the Maple code, with a short description.

Computation of the derivatives of ξ\xi

With the notation of Proposition 5.3 we have ξ(k)​(1)=2​a2​(k+1)​(k+1)!\xi^{(k)}(1)=2a_{2(k+1)}(k+1)!. Here the numbers aka_{k} are defined by

h−1​(w)=∑k=1∞ak​wk,h^{-1}(w)=\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}a_{k}w^{k},

where h−1h^{-1} is the inverse to

h⁡(z)=∑k=1∞bk​zk,h(z)=\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}b_{k}z^{k},

which satisfies (h⁡(z))2=e−z+z−1(h(z))^{2}=e^{-z}+z-1 and h′​(0)>0h^{\prime}(0)>0.

The procedure h_polynomial(n) returns the list of numbers [b1,…,bn][b_{1},\ldots,b_{n}]. These numbers are computed by equating the coefficients in the relation

(∑k=1∞bk​zk)2=∑k=2∞(−1)kk!​zk.\left(\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}b_{k}z^{k}\right)^{2}=\sum_{k=2}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^{k}}{k!}z^{k}.

We get

∑l=1k−1bl​bk−l=(−1)kk!\sum_{l=1}^{k-1}b_{l}b_{k-l}=\frac{(-1)^{k}}{k!}

for k≥2k\geq 2, from which we determine the number bk+1b_{k+1} from b1,…,bkb_{1},\ldots,b_{k}. The numbers b1,…,bnb_{1},\ldots,b_{n} are just the coefficients in the Taylor expansion of h⁡(z)h(z) at z=0z=0 up to order nn. We could therefore also have used the command taylor but we prefer the more direct and efficient method outlined in the procedure below.

h_polynomial:=proc(n)
        local b, j:
        b[1]:=1/sqrt(2):
        for j from 1 to (n-1) do
                b[j+1]:=((-1)^j/(j+2)!
                -sum(b[l+1]*b[j-l+1], l=1..(j-1)))/2/b[1]:
        end do: j:=’j’:
        return [seq(b[j], j=1..(n))];
end proc;

The procedure xi_derivatives(n) computes the numbers [ξ⁡(1),…,ξ(n−1)​(1)][\xi(1),\ldots,\xi^{(n-1)}(1)] and it uses the procedure h_polynomial. To find these numbers it is enough to determine the numbers a1,…,a2​na_{1},\ldots,a_{2n} and this we do by equating coefficients in the relation h−1​(h​(z))=zh^{-1}(h(z))=z. We put

∑l=k∞bk,l​zl=(∑l=1∞bl​zl)k.\sum_{l=k}^{\infty}b_{k,l}z^{l}=\left(\sum_{l=1}^{\infty}b_{l}z^{l}\right)^{k}.

Hence b1,l=blb_{1,l}=b_{l} for l≥1l\geq 1 and by Cauchy multiplication,

bk+1,l=∑m=kl−1bk,m​bl−m,b_{k+1,l}=\sum_{m=k}^{l-1}b_{k,m}b_{l-m},

for l≥k+1l\geq k+1. Since h−1​(h​(z))=zh^{-1}(h(z))=z we must furthermore have

z=∑k=1∞ak​(∑l=k∞bk,l​zl)=∑l=1∞(∑k=1lak​bk,l)​zl.z=\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}a_{k}\left(\sum_{l=k}^{\infty}b_{k,l}z^{l}\right)=\sum_{l=1}^{\infty}\left(\sum_{k=1}^{l}a_{k}b_{k,l}\right)z^{l}.

Therefore a1​b1,1=1a_{1}b_{1,1}=1 and

∑k=1lak​bk,l=0\sum_{k=1}^{l}a_{k}b_{k,l}=0

for l≥2l\geq 2. Hence a1=1/b1,1=1/b1a_{1}=1/b_{1,1}=1/b_{1}. The point is now that ala_{l} can be computed when we know a1,…,al−1a_{1},\ldots,a_{l-1} as well as b1,l,…,bl,lb_{1,l},\ldots,b_{l,l}. This is the main idea behind the procedure below.

xi_derivatives:=proc(N)
        local i,p,j,k,l,temp,a,h,b:
        h:=h_polynomial(2*N):
        for i from 1 to 2*N do
                for p from 1 to 2*N do
                        b[i,p]:=0:
                end do: p:=’p’:
        end do: i:=’i’:
        for j from 1 to 2*N do b[1,j]:=h[j]: end do: j:=’j’:
        a[1]:=sqrt(2):
        for k from 1 to (2*N-1) do
                for l from (k+1) to 2*N do
                        temp:=0:
                        for j from 1 to (l-1) do
                                temp:=temp+b[k,j]*h[l-j]:
                        end do: j:=’j’:
                        b[k+1,l]:=temp:
                end do: l:=’l’:
                a[k+1]:=-sum(a[m]*b[m,k+1],m=1..k)/b[k+1,k+1]:
        end do: k:=’k’:
        return [seq(2*a[2*j]*(j!),j=1..N)];
end proc;

We could also have used the command taylor to compute the coefficients in the expansion of h−1​(h​(z))h^{-1}(h(z)), but it runs very slowly, so a more efficient program is needed. We have found the derivatives of ξ\xi to be:

ξ⁡(1)\displaystyle\xi(1) =\displaystyle= 23\displaystyle\frac{2}{3}
ξ′​(1)\displaystyle\xi^{\prime}(1) =\displaystyle= 2333⋅5\displaystyle\frac{2^{3}}{3^{3}\cdot 5}
ξ(2)​(1)\displaystyle\xi^{(2)}(1) =\displaystyle= −2434⋅5⋅7\displaystyle-\frac{2^{4}}{3^{4}\cdot 5\cdot 7}
ξ(3)​(1)\displaystyle\xi^{(3)}(1) =\displaystyle= −2535⋅5⋅7\displaystyle-\frac{2^{5}}{3^{5}\cdot 5\cdot 7}
ξ(4)​(1)\displaystyle\xi^{(4)}(1) =\displaystyle= 26⋅28138⋅52⋅7⋅11\displaystyle\frac{2^{6}\cdot 281}{3^{8}\cdot 5^{2}\cdot 7\cdot 11}
ξ(5)​(1)\displaystyle\xi^{(5)}(1) =\displaystyle= 27⋅23⋅22739⋅52⋅7⋅11⋅13\displaystyle\frac{2^{7}\cdot 23\cdot 227}{3^{9}\cdot 5^{2}\cdot 7\cdot 11\cdot 13}
ξ(6)​(1)\displaystyle\xi^{(6)}(1) =\displaystyle= −28⋅53⋅103310⋅52⋅7⋅11⋅13\displaystyle-\frac{2^{8}\cdot 53\cdot 103}{3^{10}\cdot 5^{2}\cdot 7\cdot 11\cdot 13}
ξ(7)​(1)\displaystyle\xi^{(7)}(1) =\displaystyle= −29⋅373⋅4439⋅557312⋅54⋅72⋅11⋅13⋅17\displaystyle-\frac{2^{9}\cdot 373\cdot 4439\cdot 557}{3^{12}\cdot 5^{4}\cdot 7^{2}\cdot 11\cdot 13\cdot 17}
ξ(8)​(1)\displaystyle\xi^{(8)}(1) =\displaystyle= 210⋅2650986803313⋅54⋅72⋅11⋅13⋅17⋅19\displaystyle\frac{2^{10}\cdot 2650986803}{3^{13}\cdot 5^{4}\cdot 7^{2}\cdot 11\cdot 13\cdot 17\cdot 19}
ξ(9)​(1)\displaystyle\xi^{(9)}(1) =\displaystyle= 211⋅6171801683314⋅54⋅72⋅11⋅13⋅17⋅19\displaystyle\frac{2^{11}\cdot 6171801683}{3^{14}\cdot 5^{4}\cdot 7^{2}\cdot 11\cdot 13\cdot 17\cdot 19}
ξ(10)​(1)\displaystyle\xi^{(10)}(1) =\displaystyle= −212⋅1117⋅3835213201316⋅52⋅72⋅11⋅13⋅17⋅19⋅23.\displaystyle-\frac{2^{12}\cdot 1117\cdot 3835213201}{3^{16}\cdot 5^{2}\cdot 7^{2}\cdot 11\cdot 13\cdot 17\cdot 19\cdot 23}.

The asymptotic expansion of φ\varphi

The asymptotic expansion of φ⁡(x)\varphi(x) can be found from relation (11), that is

φ⁡(x)=∑k=0nξ(k)​(1)2​xk+1−∑k=1n(−1)k​xkk!​∫0φ⁡(x)(u+e−u−1)k​𝑑u+o⁡(x−(n+1)).\varphi(x)=\sum_{k=0}^{n}\frac{\xi^{(k)}(1)}{2x^{k+1}}-\sum_{k=1}^{n}\frac{(-1)^{k}x^{k}}{k!}\int_{0}^{\varphi(x)}(u+e^{-u}-1)^{k}\,du+o(x^{-(n+1)}).

We use two procedures sum_of_int(n,PHI) and xi_sum(n). The procedure sum_of_int(n,PHI) takes an expression of the form

𝙿𝙷𝙸=∑k=1mckxk\verb!PHI!=\sum_{k=1}^{m}\frac{c_{k}}{x^{k}}

and computes the sum of integrals

∑k=1n(−1)k​xkk!​∫0𝙿𝙷𝙸(u+e−u−1)k​𝑑u\sum_{k=1}^{n}\frac{(-1)^{k}x^{k}}{k!}\int_{0}^{\verb!PHI!}(u+e^{-u}-1)^{k}\,du

up to o⁡(x−(n+1))o(x^{-(n+1)}). This is done in the same way as in Lemma 4.4. We put

(e−u+u−1)k=∑l=2​k∞tk,l​ul,(e^{-u}+u-1)^{k}=\sum_{l=2k}^{\infty}t_{k,l}u^{l},

and observe that by Cauchy multiplication

tk+1,m=∑l=2m−2​k(−1)ll!​tk,m−l,t_{k+1,m}=\sum_{l=2}^{m-2k}\frac{(-1)^{l}}{l!}t_{k,m-l},

for m≥2​(k+1)m\geq 2(k+1). Since t1,m=(−1)m/m!t_{1,m}=(-1)^{m}/m! we can compute the numbers tk,⋅t_{k,\cdot} from the numbers tk−1,⋅t_{k-1,\cdot} for k≥2k\geq 2. The numbers tk,⋅t_{k,\cdot} are then used to approximate the integrand (u+e−u−1)k(u+e^{-u}-1)^{k} by its Taylor polynomial centered at u=0u=0 of order n+kn+k.

sum_of_int:=proc(n,PHI)
        local l,t,T,s,k,m,j,temp,temp1:
        for l from 2 to (n+1) do
                t[1,l]:=(-1)^l/l!:
        end do: l:=’l’:
        T:=sum(t[1,l]*PHI^(l+1)/(l+1), l=2..(n+1)):
        s:=-x*T:Ψ
        for k from 2 to n do
                T:=0:
                for m from 2*k to (n+k) do
                        t[k,m]:=
                        sum((-1)^l/l!*t[k-1,m-l], l=2..(m-2*k+2)):
                        T:=T+t[k,m]*PHI^(m+1)/(m+1):
                end do: m:=’m’:
                s:=s+(-1)^k*x^k/k!*T:
        end do: k:=’k’:
        temp:=subs(x=1/x,expand(s)):
        temp1:=0:
        for j from 0 to (n+1) do
                temp1:=temp1+coeff(temp,x,j)*x^(-j):
        end do: j:=’j’:
        return temp1;Ψ
end proc;

We notice that the variable s in the procedure sum_of_int(n,PHI) contains many terms of order x−lx^{-l} with l>kl>k. These terms are not needed and they are therefore deleted. That happens in the for loop containing temp1. (It improves program efficiency.)

The second procedure xi_sum(n+1) simply computes the asymptotic expansion

∑k=0nξ(k)​(1)2​xk+1\sum_{k=0}^{n}\frac{\xi^{(k)}(1)}{2x^{k+1}}

by calling the procedure xi_derivatives(n+1).

xi_sum:=proc(n)
        local temp:
        temp:=xi_derivatives(n):
        return sum(temp[k]/2/x^k, k=1..n);
end proc;

To find the expansion of φ⁡(x)\varphi(x) we combine these two procedures in the procedure asymp_phi(n). This procedure computes the asymptotic expansion of φ⁡(x)\varphi(x) up to order o⁡(x−n−1)o(x^{-n-1}).

asymp_phi:=proc(n)
        local phi,k:
        phi:=1/3/x:
        for k from 1 to n do
                phi:=xi_sum(k+1)-sum_of_int(k,phi):
        end do:
        return phi;
end proc;

We have

φ⁡(x)=∑k=110ckxk+o⁡(x−10),\varphi(x)=\sum_{k=1}^{10}\frac{c_{k}}{x^{k}}+o(x^{-10}),

where

c1\displaystyle c_{1} =\displaystyle= 13\displaystyle\frac{1}{3}

The asymptotic expansion of mm

Since m⁡(x)=x​e−φ⁡(x)m(x)=xe^{-\varphi(x)} it is easy to find the asymptotic expansion of m⁡(x)m(x) when we have the asymptotic expansion of φ⁡(x)\varphi(x). It is done in the procedure asymp_m(n), that gives the expansion of m⁡(x)m(x) up to order x1−nx^{1-n}.

asymp_m:=proc(n)
        local temp:
        temp:=subs(x=1/x, asymp_phi(n)):
        temp:=convert(taylor(exp(-temp), x=0, n+2), polynom):
        temp:=subs(x=1/x,temp):
        return expand(x*temp);
end proc;

We have

m⁡(x)=x−13+∑k=19mkxk+o⁡(x−9),m(x)=x-\frac{1}{3}+\sum_{k=1}^{9}\frac{m_{k}}{x^{k}}+o(x^{-9}),
